solutions.check: 30 entries verified against the grid (lengths, crossings, linked-clue mapping)

clue.text: Unconvinced about church's involvement in plastic surgery

blocks.note: PLASTIC rearranged, split S…PTICAL around the church

explanation.surface: A sceptic wonders why the church is getting mixed up in cosmetic surgery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plastic surgery' reads as one phrase, but it splits: PLASTIC is the fodder and 'surgery' is what is done to it.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone sceptical is unconvinced by what they are told.

clue.text: Sub-continent of America lifted controversial technology ban

indicators.note: in a down clue, lifting the letters reads them bottom to top

explanation.surface: America scraps its ban on a controversial technology, a lift that reaches as far as a whole sub-continent.
explanation.walkthrough: The pieces are gathered in the order A, BAR, AI as the clue gives them, then the whole string is read upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: The Arabian peninsula is large enough to be called a sub-continent.

clue.text: I'm not wasting time mixing with people sought by Biden and Trump

definitions.note: the definition describes the thing both candidates sought rather than naming it

indicators.note: T (time) is wasted, i.e. lost, from I'M NOT
the letters are stirred together into a new order

explanation.surface: A voter refuses to waste time mingling with the crowds chasing Biden and Trump.
explanation.walkthrough: Both men sought their party's nomination for the US presidency.
explanation.definitionFit: Biden and Trump each sought their party's nomination to run for president.

clue.text: Labour needs good, Balls-free, backing to get in fair and square

indicators.note: in a down clue, the letters run backwards
the result goes inside the other piece

blocks.note: TRUE = fair and square, opened to take the middle
GOOD minus its two Os gives GD, then reversed

explanation.surface: A dig at the Labour party and Ed Balls: it needs good backing, without him, to win fairly.
explanation.walkthrough: Balls is Ed Balls, the former Labour shadow chancellor, and the capital letter hides that here it just means the letter O.
explanation.definitionFit: To trudge is to labour along, walking heavily and with effort.

clue.text: Party turning on agent

explanation.surface: A political party turns on one of its own operatives.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Agent' suggests a spy or operative; here it has its root sense, one who acts.
explanation.definitionFit: Agent in its root sense, from Latin agere, to do: the one who performs an action.

clue.text: Many a government policy is savagely satirised, with loss of ego

indicators.note: the letters are savaged into a new order
ego = I, and one I is lost

explanation.surface: A satirist's boast that most government policies get savagely mocked in the magazine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Is' looks like part of the fodder but is only the link; SATIRISED has two Is and loses one.
explanation.definitionFit: The joke is that many government policies turn out to be disasters.

clue.text: King Brian nominally over this panic?

blocks.note: what a figurehead king reigns over in name only
a flustered condition, as in the British 'get in a ...'

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a pompous figure dubbed King Brian is behind the current panic.
explanation.walkthrough: A king nominally rules over a STATE; and to be 'in a state' in Britain is to be in a panic.
explanation.definitionFit: A realm by example, what a monarch reigns over; and a British idiom for agitation.

clue.text: Wow! Trump's first half barrier!

blocks.note: cor! is a British exclamation of surprise

explanation.surface: An exclamation at Trump building his barrier, the border wall.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trump's first half' is not the first half of the word TRUMP but of his first name, Donald.
explanation.definitionFit: A cordon is a line of police or tape forming a barrier.

clue.text: Bum, lacking energy, is not turning into criminal

indicators.note: the letters are turned into a new order

blocks.note: ARSE, a British word for bum, minus E

explanation.surface: A lazy layabout who can't be bothered to change is becoming a crook.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bum' reads as a layabout, but it is the backside, and only the British spelling ARSE gives the right letters.
explanation.definitionFit: An arsonist is a criminal who deliberately sets fires.

clue.text: Ranch hand who'll give you an reliable erection

definitions.text: who'll give you an reliable erection

blocks.note: one who herds cattle on a ranch

blocks.clueFragment: who'll give you an reliable erection
blocks.note: a rogue builder, whose erections are buildings

explanation.surface: A smutty advert promising a dependable erection from a ranch hand.
explanation.walkthrough: The printed 'an reliable' has surely lost 'un': a cowboy, in Britain, is a rogue tradesman whose erections, buildings, are unreliable.
explanation.definitionFit: A cowboy is both a ranch hand and a slapdash builder.

clue.text: (&12ac.) Out with organisation! Do what Sunak's government suspiciously rushed through

definitions.text: what Sunak's government suspiciously rushed through

blocks.note: to perform or do something, a three-letter verb

explanation.surface: A protest cry to get out and organise against a law the government rushed through.
explanation.walkthrough: The Public Order Act 2023 gave British police new powers against protest; the answer runs on into 12 across.
explanation.definitionFit: The Public Order Act 2023 was pushed through Parliament by Rishi Sunak's government.

clue.text: see 11ac.
Trump's article in vain – crap

definitions.note: the definition is possessive: Ivana was Trump's, his first wife

indicators.note: crap as an adjective means badly done, so the letters are scrambled

explanation.surface: A sneer that Trump's article, whatever it is, is vain rubbish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' is not a container indicator here; the article joins VAIN and all five letters are mixed.
explanation.definitionFit: Ivana Trump was Donald Trump's first wife, so she was Trump's.

clue.text: Pot makes you piss good in Hamburg

blocks.note: piss is British slang for weak beer

explanation.surface: A warning that smoking pot makes you wet yourself in Hamburg.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pot' pretends to be cannabis and 'piss' to be urinating; they are a belly and beer.
explanation.definitionFit: Pot is short for pot belly, a round paunch of the kind heavy drinking produces.

clue.text: Olive might eff off!

blocks.note: olives are often filled with pimento

explanation.surface: Someone called Olive might tell you where to go.
explanation.walkthrough: Olive looks like a woman's name, but the capital is only there because it starts the clue: the fruit gets stuffed.
explanation.definitionFit: Two British idioms of dismissal, both euphemisms for a ruder word; and literally what happens to an olive.

clue.text: Stiff finally, you pay special attention at climax

indicators.note: take the final letter of the word next to it

explanation.surface: A bawdy line about something stiff and the attention it needs at the climax.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Finally' looks like it belongs to 'Stiff', but it points forward to 'you'.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: what will not bend is stiff, literally or in attitude.

clue.text: Fail dismally to rein in politician – Tory's last boost

explanation.surface: A failed attempt to keep an MP in check, and a Tory's final push.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fail dismally' reads as a single phrase for flopping, but 'dismally' is the instruction to jumble FAIL.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, most familiar from sound: an amplifier boosts a signal.

clue.text: Soldier to be killed takes shilling – bliss!

blocks.note: s = shilling, an old British coin

explanation.surface: A doomed soldier who took the King's shilling, on enlisting, finds it bliss.
explanation.walkthrough: Taking the King's shilling was the old British phrase for enlisting in the army.
explanation.definitionFit: Paradise, the heaven of scripture, stands by extension for any perfect happiness.

clue.text: Much experienced, but put off having to go topless in transit?

indicators.note: the top, first, letter is removed
the result goes inside the van

blocks.note: a Transit is a Ford van, common in Britain

blocks.clueFragment: put off having to go topless

explanation.surface: A seasoned traveller put off by having to strip to the waist in transit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Transit' reads as travelling, but the Ford Transit is a van, and the capital is disguised.
explanation.definitionFit: Veteran works as an adjective too, as in a veteran campaigner, meaning long-practised.

clue.text: So, one Labour leader should be put inside? Quite right!

indicators.note: 'put inside' is slang for jailing someone

blocks.note: very = so, as in so good

explanation.surface: Someone argues that a Labour leader should be jailed, and another agrees heartily.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Labour leader' pretends to be Keir Starmer; it is just L, the first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Verily is an old word meaning truly, said in agreement like quite right.

clue.text: 'Dashed ball hosted by bounder' creates bad feeling

blocks.note: a cur, like a bounder, is a scoundrel

explanation.surface: A newspaper headline about a scandalous party where a cad was the host.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dashed' could be the old British expletive; it is the plain verb, ran.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: rancour is lasting bitterness, feeling gone sour.

clue.text: Openly gay and keen for public disapproval?

blocks.note: to be out is to be openly gay
to keen is to wail, cry in grief

explanation.surface: Coming out and being eager for the public to object.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Keen' reads as eager; the verb to keen, lament, is what counts.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the public crying out against something.

clue.text: Crap, having swallowed second drug sample

explanation.surface: A bad batch of drugs taken for testing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Swallowed' and 'drug' paint someone taking pills; the swallowing is TAT enclosing S.
explanation.definitionFit: Noun or verb: a taste is a small sample, and to taste is to sample.

clue.text: Each male in the pen is lustful

blocks.note: a sty is a pen for pigs

explanation.surface: A claim that every man in prison is randy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The pen' looks like the penitentiary; it is a pigsty.
explanation.definitionFit: Steamy means erotic, full of lust.

clue.text: Pence: simple prig

blocks.note: rude = simple, primitive, as in a rude hut

explanation.surface: A verdict on Mike Pence, Trump's vice president: a simple-minded prude.
explanation.walkthrough: Pence is Mike Pence, known for his strict morals, but he supplies only the P.
explanation.definitionFit: A prig is a prudish, self-righteous person.

clue.text: Bar with nothing to separate opposing US parties

indicators.note: to separate two things is to come between them

explanation.surface: A bar that keeps America's two warring parties apart.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bar' could be a verb, to block; it is the noun, a length of metal.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a straight length of metal or wood.

clue.text: It felt bad playing around the French combat zone

indicators.note: the letters play about into a new order

explanation.surface: A player who felt awful playing in France.
explanation.walkthrough: Strictly, LE goes inside the jumbled letters, but the enumeration needs all eleven mixed together.
explanation.definitionFit: A battlefield is the zone where combat takes place.

clue.text: Profitable company hoards lithium – sign of peak activity?

blocks.note: Li is the chemical symbol for lithium

explanation.surface: An oil giant stockpiling lithium as a signal that business is booming.
explanation.walkthrough: A blip is a peak on a screen trace; the question mark flags the double sense of 'peak activity'.
explanation.definitionFit: A blip is a spike on a monitor, a sign of activity peaking.

clue.text: Cyclops wearing Tramp's briefs

indicators.note: I is worn inside the tramps' letters

explanation.surface: The one-eyed setter dressed in a tramp's underpants.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tramp's' reads as tramp is; 'briefs' pretend to be pants but are sets of papers.
explanation.definitionFit: Dossiers are files of papers, briefs on a subject.

clue.text: Crew members come around one?

explanation.surface: Sailors arriving together, with a smutty undertone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Come around' reads as a visit; the question mark warns that 'come' is being taken crudely.
explanation.definitionFit: Sailors by trade, the men who crew a ship.
